warriors.name: Imp
warriors.inspiredBy: Recreates Imp by A. K. Dewdney, from the first Core War article (Scientific American, May 1984). The original is the same single instruction.
warriors.summary: The smallest possible warrior: one instruction that copies itself into the next cell and then runs that copy. It crawls through the core forever.
how: MOV.I $0, $1 copies the whole instruction at offset 0 (itself) to offset 1.
The process moves on to the next cell, which now holds the same instruction, and the cycle repeats.
When the Imp crawls over enemy code it replaces it with Imp. Enemy processes that reach those cells turn into Imps too, which is why Imp battles usually end in ties.
strengths: Almost impossible to kill: a bomb behind it does nothing, and it moves every cycle.
Turns a likely loss into a tie, which still scores 1 point.
weaknesses: Never kills anything by itself.
One DAT written just ahead of it ends it, and scanners find it easily.
warriors.tryIt: Run Imp against itself. Why can neither one ever win?

warriors.name: Dwarf
warriors.inspiredBy: Recreates Dwarf by A. K. Dewdney (1984), the original bomber. The JavaScript and Python versions in the library generate exactly the same code.
warriors.summary: The classic stone: a three-instruction loop that drops a DAT bomb on every fourth cell of the core.
how: bomb's B-field is a pointer. ADD.AB #4, bomb moves it four cells further each pass.
MOV.I bomb, @bomb copies the bomb to wherever that pointer points (@ means use the B-field as an address).
Any enemy process that later executes one of those DATs dies.
4 divides 8000, so the bombs only ever land a multiple of 4 cells from bomb. The other three instructions are 1, 2 and 3 cells away, so the Dwarf never hits itself.
strengths: Tiny (4 cells), so it's hard to find and hard to hit.
Gets through the whole core in 6,000 cycles, quickly enough to beat most scanners.
weaknesses: Replicators make copies faster than it can bomb them.
Leaves gaps of three cells, so very small enemies can survive between bombs.
warriors.tryIt: Change step to 3 and run it alone (one warrior). It eventually kills itself. Work out when.

warriors.name: Gemini
warriors.inspiredBy: Based on Gemini by A. K. Dewdney (1984), the first published program that copies itself. This version uses ICWS'94 post-increment modes to do it in a much shorter loop.
warriors.summary: Copies its entire body 100 cells ahead, then jumps into the copy. It is the ancestor of every replicator, but this one only moves; it doesn't multiply.
how: ptr holds two pointers relative to itself: the A-field is the next cell to read, the B-field the next cell to write.
MOV.I }ptr, >ptr copies one cell and then increments both pointers. That is the whole copy loop body.
Because ICWS'94 copies the source instruction before incrementing, the copy of ptr itself starts with clean pointers.
SEQ.A #len, ptr stops the loop after len cells; JMP copy+hop continues execution inside the new copy.
strengths: Leaves a dead copy behind at every hop, which makes scanners waste time on decoys.
weaknesses: Still only one process: a single bomb on the live copy kills it.
Spends all its time moving and never attacks. It ranks last in the library benchmark.
warriors.tryIt: Add an SPL so the old copy keeps running as well. You have just reinvented the replicator.

warriors.name: Mice
warriors.inspiredBy: Adapted from MICE by Chip Wendell, winner of the first ICWS tournament in 1986, rewritten in ICWS'94 syntax with explicit modifiers.
warriors.summary: A replicator ("paper"). It copies its 8 instructions to a new place, starts a process there with SPL, then does it again somewhere else. Every copy does the same, so the number of copies grows exponentially.
how: MOV.AB #12, ptr sets a counter of cells to copy.
MOV.I @ptr, <copy copies one cell. The source is ptr + counter; the destination is copy's B-field after it has been decremented. The copy is built from the end backwards.
DJN.B loop, ptr decrements the counter and repeats until it reaches zero.
SPL.B @copy, 0 starts a new process at the new copy, and ADD.AB #653, copy picks a fresh destination for the next one.
strengths: Bombers can't kill copies as fast as they appear.
Ends with thousands of processes in dozens of places.
weaknesses: Each copy takes about 30 cycles to build: slow next to silk papers.
Scanners that stun before clearing (Seeker, Two-Pass Clear) beat it.
warriors.tryIt: Watch the Processes chart while Mice fights Dwarf, and find the moment the curve takes off.

warriors.name: Imp Ring
warriors.inspiredBy: Uses the idea behind The IMPire strikes back by Anders Ivner (October 1992), described in Steven Morrell's My First Corewar Book as the first imp ring.
warriors.summary: Three imps exactly a third of the core apart, executing in turn. Each writes the cell the next imp is about to execute, so the three move as one unit.
how: The imp is MOV.I #0, 2667. It copies itself 2667 cells ahead, and 3 × 2667 = 8001, one cell past where it started.
The launcher turns 1 process into 4 with two SPL 1s, then each passes through JMP }tab, which sends successive processes to successive table entries.
Three table entries jump to the three ring points in order, and the fourth process dies on a DAT.
Point 0 writes point 1 just before point 1 runs, point 1 writes point 2, and point 2 writes point 0 plus one cell. Order is everything.
strengths: Ties or beats most stones: it overwrites their code with imp as it passes through.
Much harder to stop than a single Imp.
weaknesses: Rarely wins outright against papers or clears.
Breaks if the processes get out of order, for example if an enemy SPL lands in the ring.
warriors.tryIt: Change step to 2666. Why does the ring fall apart?

warriors.name: Stone and Imp
warriors.inspiredBy: A simplified take on the stone/imp design of Cannonade (Paul Kline), Blue Funk (Steven Morrell) and Impfinity (Damien Doligez), all '94 hill champions.
warriors.summary: Splits into two warriors at once: a Dwarf-style stone and an Imp Ring. The stone hunts, and the imps turn would-be losses into ties.
how: SPL stone sends one process to the bomber; the rest launch an imp ring exactly as Imp Ring does.
All four processes share the warrior's turns, so the stone bombs at a quarter of the Dwarf's speed.
Imps move through the stone's code and turn it into imp. In this version the stone doesn't last long once the ring comes round.
strengths: Rarely loses outright: the ring survives most attacks.
weaknesses: Slower than either part alone. In the benchmark it does worse than plain Imp Ring.
Real stone/imps "boot" (copy) the stone away from the ring and pick the imp step so their bombs never break the ring. This version doesn't.
warriors.tryIt: Move the stone out of the ring's path: copy it 4000 cells away before starting it. Does the score improve?

warriors.name: Silk
warriors.inspiredBy: Uses the trick from Silk Warrior and TimeScape by Juha Pohjalainen (1994–95), the papers that gave "silk" its name. Paperone by Beppe Bezzi is another well-known example.
warriors.summary: A replicator with no copy loop. Eight processes run the same two instructions in lockstep; each copies one cell and starts one process in the copy, so a whole new copy appears in a single pass.
how: Three SPL 1s turn 1 process into 8, all queued at silk in order.
Each of the 8 runs SPL step, starting a process at the copy location. Then each runs MOV.I >silk, }silk, copying the next cell.
The processes in the copy run just behind the copying, so each instruction arrives just before they need it. It's the same timing trick the Imp Ring uses.
ADD.A and MOV.F pick a new distance and reset the pointers, and the 8 processes loop to make another copy.
strengths: Top of the library benchmark.
Makes a new copy every few cycles, so it reaches thousands of processes almost immediately.
weaknesses: Rarely wins quickly against an Imp: lots of ties.
Vulnerable to SPL 0 carpets followed by a clear, which is how the '94 hill's scanners eventually beat it.
warriors.tryIt: Add a third line, MOV.I bomb, >2000, so every copy also bombs. That makes it a paper/stone. Does it beat Mice faster?

warriors.name: Papercut
warriors.inspiredBy: Bombing silk papers such as Paperone (Beppe Bezzi, 1995) and Silk Warrior 1.3 (Juha Pohjalainen, 1994). Written for ZoreWars and tuned with zorewars tune.
warriors.summary: A silk paper that bombs while it spreads. Sixteen processes copy the warrior to a new spot on every pass, and each pass also drops a DAT bomb somewhere else in the core.
how: Four SPL 1 lines turn one process into 16. All 16 run the silk loop in step, one instruction each.
SPL STEP, #0 and MOV.I >silk, }silk copy the warrior one cell per process and start the copy running: 16 processes copy 16 cells.
MOV.I seed, >carpet drops a bomb, and the two ADDs move both the bomb pointer and the next copy distance, so neither falls into a pattern.
MOV.F seed, silk resets the copy pointers and the loop starts again in the new copy.
strengths: Hard to kill: every copy is a full warrior, so a bomb only takes out one of many.
The bombs give it some kill power against stones and other papers, which pure silks lack.
weaknesses: Scanners that stun with SPL carpets (Gatekeeper, Blur) catch the copies and freeze them.
Papers rarely kill fast, so many rounds end in ties against other papers and imps.
warriors.tryIt: The constants at the top came from node cli/zorewars.js tune warriors/papercut.js. Change STEP to 1777 and watch it against Gatekeeper, then retune it yourself.

warriors.name: Fast Silk
warriors.inspiredBy: The small multi-stream papers inside modern paper/stone warriors such as Azathoth (John Metcalf). Written from scratch for ZoreWars and tuned with zorewars tune.
warriors.summary: A 10-instruction silk paper. Each process copies three cells per pass instead of one, so four processes copy the whole body in a single pass and start the copy. It has no bombs at all, and it was our best warrior against the strongest classics when it was added.
how: Two SPL 1 lines make four processes. All four run the loop in step, one instruction each.
SPL STEP, #0 starts a process in the copy; three MOV.I >silk, }silk lines copy three cells each, so four processes copy twelve cells: more than the 8-line body.
ADD.A #DELTA, seed changes the copy distance for the next pass, and MOV.F seed, silk resets the pointers.
Compare Papercut: 7 instructions per pass to copy one cell per process, plus bombs. Fast Silk spends 6 to copy three.
strengths: Tiny and fast: copies spread over the core within a few thousand cycles and are hard to find.
Holds its own against the modern paper/stone hill leaders (about a point per round against Azathoth and Arvon).
weaknesses: No kill power of its own: most rounds against other papers are ties.
SPL-carpet scanners such as Myrmidon freeze its copies.
warriors.tryIt: Set MOVS: 2. The generator refuses until you raise LEVELS, because four processes copying two cells each can't cover the body.

warriors.name: Evolved Silk
warriors.inspiredBy: Bred by zorewars evolve, which runs Red Queen rounds of MAP-Elites as in Digital Red Queen (Sakana AI and MIT), starting from slices of ZoreWars bots. Nobody wrote it.
warriors.summary: A silk paper that evolution put together from fragments of other warriors. It turned up in the evolver's archive cell for warriors that reach the process limit, and it is a recognisable classic design: a silk whose copy distance changes on every pass.
how: Six SPL lines make the processes. One of them, SPL $31, starts a process in empty core where it dies at once: a harmless leftover of evolution.
SPL $1777, #0 and MOV.I >-1, }-1 are the silk: every process copies one cell of the warrior 1777 cells away and starts the copy.
ADD.A #1013, seed changes the copy distance by 1013 each pass, so the copies spread out instead of following one stride.
MOV.F seed, silk resets the pointers for the next pass.
strengths: Only 12 instructions, and it fills the core with copies within a few thousand cycles.
Shows what the evolver can find on its own: the same idea human players arrived at in 1994.
weaknesses: It never bombs, so it can't kill anything that doesn't run into its copies. Most rounds against other papers are ties.
SPL-carpet scanners freeze it, like any silk.
warriors.tryIt: Delete the SPL $31 line and see whether it does any better. Then run node cli/zorewars.js species warriors/evolvedsilk.red to see its niche.

warriors.name: Twin Silk
warriors.inspiredBy: Inspired by the survival papers that lead the 10-player arena of ModelWar, such as John Metcalf's paper with silk-imps, but built from ZoreWars' own Silk. Its constants came from a random search in a local copy of that arena.
warriors.summary: Two Silk papers at once. One boot splits into two groups of eight processes, and each group runs its own silk loop with its own copy distance and drift, so the two families of copies spread over different parts of the core.
how: SPL b sends one process to paper B; three SPL 1s on each side make eight processes per paper.
Each paper is the Silk loop: SPL step, #0 starts a process in the copy and MOV.I >silk, }silk copies one cell per process.
Paper A starts 718 cells away and drifts by 725 a pass; paper B starts 4315 away and drifts by 3173, so their copies rarely land on each other.
Nothing bombs: in a many-warrior game a round's points are shared by the survivors, so staying alive is worth more than killing.
strengths: Survives about nine rounds in ten in a crowded 10-warrior arena, where scanners, stones and clears mostly die.
A clear that wipes one paper's copies rarely finds all of the other's.
weaknesses: No kill power: against other papers and imps it ties.
Imp-spiral survivors such as Tsunami outlast it slightly, and SPL-carpet scanners freeze silks.
warriors.tryIt: Run it in a crowd: node cli/zorewars.js battle warriors/twinsilk.red warriors/silk.red warriors/stoneimp.red warriors/gatekeeper.js -r 50. Then delete paper B (and SPL b) and see how much survival you lose.

warriors.name: Red Queen
warriors.inspiredBy: Our evolver came upon this warrior, but its parts have a history. The replicator is Mice by Chip Wendell, winner of the first ICWS tournament in 1986, here unchanged. The scanner is Gatekeeper, ZoreWars' compare scanner in the line of Iron Gate (Wayne Sheppard) and Agony (Stefan Strack). The evolver (zorewars evolve, after Digital Red Queen by Sakana AI and MIT) found the pairing in a run that started from Hedgehog, Hydra and Fast Silk.
warriors.summary: Our evolver came upon it: Gatekeeper and a complete copy of Chip Wendell's Mice, started side by side with one extra SPL. It was the strongest ZoreWars warrior when it was added, both overall and against the Hall of Fame classics. That surprised us, because our hand-built scanner/paper hybrids had failed.
how: Three launch lines: two SPLs start Mice and a leftover fragment, then a JMP sends the first process into Gatekeeper.
Gatekeeper runs unchanged: it compares cells across the core, stuns anything it finds with a carpet of SPL 0, and finishes with a two-pass clear.
Mice copies itself 653 cells further on, starts a process in the copy, and repeats. Each copy adds only one process.

Why it works when our hand-built hybrids didn't: a warrior gets one instruction per turn, however many processes it has. Papercut runs 16 processes, so in Gatepaper the scanner got one turn in 17. Mice grows one process at a time, so Gatekeeper keeps most of the turns while the copies spread in the background.
The last three lines are a leftover of evolution: one process writes two cells and then runs off into empty core.
strengths: Our best overall and against the classics when it was added: about 1.6 points per round against the whole hill, 1.4 against the classics.
The scanner beats papers and the replicator survives the stones that beat scanners.
weaknesses: Gatekeeper's carpets also hit Mice's copies, and its final clear wipes them.
Modern paper/stone warriors such as Son of Vain still beat it most of the time.
warriors.tryIt: Delete the first two lines and change ORG to start at the JMP: that is plain Gatekeeper. Compare the two with node cli/zorewars.js hill warriors/redqueen.red --classics.

warriors.name: Scout
warriors.inspiredBy: A minimal B-field scanner in the spirit of B-scanners live in vain (Matt Hastings, 1993), which checks for non-zero fields instead of comparing pairs of cells.
warriors.summary: Looks at every 9th cell and only bombs when it finds something non-empty. Checks the distance to every find so it never bombs itself.
how: ADD.AB #9, ptr moves the probe.
JMZ.F loop, @ptr goes back to scanning if both fields of the probed cell are zero (empty core, or the scanner's own bombs).
SLT.AB #len, ptr skips the next line if the hit is further away than our own code. Otherwise JMP loop ignores it.
MOV.I bomb, @ptr drops a DAT on the hit.
strengths: Doesn't waste bombs on empty space.
A good first example of a warrior that makes decisions.
weaknesses: One bomb per hit is rarely enough against an 8-cell replicator.
Can't see enemy instructions whose A- and B-fields are both zero, such as JMP 0 or SPL 0: to JMZ.F they look like empty core.
warriors.tryIt: Delete the SLT line and run Scout alone. Find the cycle where it kills itself.

warriors.name: Seeker
warriors.inspiredBy: Follows the classic CMP-scanner pattern (compare, stun, clear) of Iron Gate (Wayne Sheppard, first in the Hall of Fame of Core Warrior #4) and Agony II (Stefan Strack). The name "scissors" comes from Matthew Householder's Scissors (1990).
warriors.summary: Compares two cells 6 apart. Empty core is identical everywhere, so any difference means an enemy. Both cells get an SPL 0 stun bomb, and after one lap a DAT sweep finishes off whatever was stunned.
how: SEQ.I compares two whole instructions. If they match, the next line is skipped and scanning continues.
ADD.F inc, scan moves both of scan's pointers 12 cells per pass, so the pair of probes covers the core every 6 cells.
A hit drops SPL #0 on both cells. An enemy process that runs it splits into copies of itself that do nothing, using up all of that warrior's turns.
The assembler computes count so the scan stops just before it would see Seeker's own code. Then MOV.I kill, >cptr clears the core.
strengths: Beats replicators like Mice: stun first, kill second.
Beats single-process warriors that sit still.
weaknesses: Loses to Silk, whose copies appear faster than it scans.
Imps slip past: an Imp in a stunned spot just keeps crawling.
warriors.tryIt: Try step 8, gap 4. Any 4-cell warrior is now always found. What does it cost?

warriors.name: Gatekeeper
warriors.inspiredBy: Compare scanners with SPL carpets and an imp gate, in the line of Iron Gate (Wayne Sheppard, 1993) and Agony II (Stefan Strack, 1995). Written for ZoreWars and tuned with zorewars tune.
warriors.summary: Compares pairs of cells across the core. Whenever a pair differs, it buries the spot under a carpet of SPL 0 stun bombs. After one lap it clears the whole core twice, first with SPL and then with DAT, and keeps decrementing an imp gate in front of itself.
how: ADD.F inc, scan moves both compare pointers STEP cells on; SEQ.I compares two cells GAP apart and skips the jump when they match (both empty).
On a difference it points bptr BACK cells before the find and writes CARPET copies of SPL.B #0, #0 there. Enemy processes that run into them stop doing anything useful and multiply uselessly.
DJN counts the scans down. The count is worked out by the assembler (EQU) so the scan never compares its own code.

After the lap comes a SPL clear over the whole core, then a DAT clear that kills the stunned processes. The final loop, JMP clr2, <gate, also decrements the cell in front of it, which stops imps crawling in.
strengths: Beats papers: stunned copies stop copying, and the DAT clear finishes them.
The best ZoreWars bot against the 34 Hall of Fame classics when it was added.
weaknesses: Stones bomb faster than it scans, and a lucky bomb on its 24 instructions ends it.
Decoys and fast-moving warriors waste its carpets.
warriors.tryIt: Run node cli/zorewars.js hill warriors/gatekeeper.js to see where it loses, then try CARPET: 8.

warriors.name: One-Shot
warriors.inspiredBy: Built the way one-shots such as Frontwards (Steven Morrell, 1995) and Myrmidon (Roy van Rijn) work: scan only until the first find, then commit everything to a clear.
warriors.summary: Scans until it finds the enemy once, then stops scanning for good. From just before the hit to the end of the core it writes SPL 0, then goes over the same stretch again with DAT.
how: Same probe pair as Seeker: SEQ.I on two cells 6 apart, moving 12 per pass.
On a hit, MOV.AB scan, cptr and ADD.AB turn the probe's address (relative to scan) into one relative to cptr, 8 cells early.
JMN.B stun, cptr keeps the stun pass going until the pointer wraps round to cptr itself, just before our own code.
MOV.B start, cptr rewinds, and the DAT pass runs until it gets stuck rewriting cptr, which stops it safely.

Each pass starts with SPL #0, 0: a swarm of processes runs the clear, so a single bomb on it can't stop it (an idea from John Metcalf's Oneshot '88). That lifted it from 1.23 to 1.34 points per round against the library and the classics.
strengths: Second in the library benchmark.
Spends no time bombing empty core.
weaknesses: Only clears from the hit forward. A paper with copies behind the hit survives, which is why Silk beats it.
Can't hurt an Imp: one cell of difference isn't enough to catch it.
warriors.tryIt: Change MOV.B start, cptr to MOV.AB start, cptr. That one-letter mistake made the first draft of this warrior lose every game. Find out why with Step and the Inspector.

warriors.name: Quickscan
warriors.inspiredBy: The quickscan technique: early prototypes by Brant Thomsen (1994), made famous by Thermite II (Robert Macrae, 1996), first in the Core Warrior #50 Hall of Fame. Modern hill leaders such as Arvon still open with one.
warriors.summary: Spends its first few dozen cycles checking 14 fixed pairs of locations spread across the core. If any pair isn't empty, it carpet-bombs that spot immediately; otherwise it becomes a Dwarf.
how: Written in JavaScript because nobody wants to work out 56 relative addresses by hand. The for loop unrolls the probes and computes each offset from the line number.
Each probe is four lines: SNE.I on a pair of cells; JMP to the next probe if they're equal; otherwise MOV.AB to aim the pointer and JMP attack.
The attack drops GAP + 12 bombs in a row over the hit, then falls through into the stone.
Open the Compiled Redcode panel in the arena to see what the generator produced.
strengths: Kills a large, slow warrior in the first hundred cycles, before it gets going.
Shows what a generator language is good for.
weaknesses: 63 instructions long, so it's a big target.
Only finds enemies sitting on one of its 28 probe cells. Against Mice it nearly always misses and loses.
warriors.tryIt: Raise PROBES to 20 and recompile. The generator recomputes every address. Mind the 100-instruction limit.

warriors.name: Blitz
warriors.inspiredBy: The quickscan opening of Thermite II (Robert Macrae, 1996), followed by a paper as in many quickscan/paper hybrids.
warriors.summary: Spends its first cycles checking 9 pairs of cells spread over the core. If a pair isn't empty, it carpet-bombs the area, first with SPL stun bombs and then with DAT. Either way it then turns into Papercut.
how: A JavaScript loop writes one SNE.I per probe. Each compares two cells GAP apart and jumps to the attack when they differ.
The attack aims ptr just before the find, writes CARPET SPL bombs, steps back and writes CARPET DAT bombs over the same cells.
Then it runs the same silk-with-bombs loop as Papercut.
strengths: Kills slow starters outright before they spread.
Still has a paper's resilience for the rest of the round.
weaknesses: 56 instructions make a big target for stones.
The probes cover only a small part of the core, so in most rounds the quickscan finds nothing.
warriors.tryIt: Set PROBES to 6 and watch the opening against Dwarf with Step.

warriors.name: Vampire
warriors.inspiredBy: The vampire idea goes back to PIPER (1987) and was refined in Sucker (Stefan Strack, 1992) and myVamp (Magnus Paulsson, 1995). Their pits hold an SPL 0 and a clear; this one uses a plain DAT.
warriors.summary: Bombs with JMP instructions ("fangs") instead of DAT. Wherever a fang lands, its target is adjusted to point back at the vampire's pit, so an enemy process that runs into one gets dragged there.
how: step is DAT #-7, #7: ADD.F step, fang moves the fang's B-field 7 forward and its A-field 7 back.
MOV.I fang, @fang drops a copy of the fang where its B-field points.
The A-field always shrinks by the same amount that the drop distance grows, so the dropped JMP always points exactly at pit.
Captured processes run the pit. Here that's a DAT, so they die.
strengths: One fang can capture every process that passes through it, not just one.
With a better pit, captured processes do the vampire's work for it.
weaknesses: With a DAT pit it's just a slower Dwarf.
Step 7 doesn't divide 8000, so eventually it bites its own code.
warriors.tryIt: Replace the pit with SPL 0 followed by a clear loop. Captured processes then waste the enemy's turns while running your clear.

warriors.name: Sweeper
warriors.inspiredBy: The simplest core clear. Later designs, such as Björn Günzel's d-clear (credited in Core Warrior #66), make the same idea harder to disrupt.
warriors.summary: Writes DAT over every cell of the core in order, then stops safely without touching its own code.
how: MOV.I bomb, >ptr writes a bomb at ptr + ptr.B and then increments the B-field. Clear and advance in one instruction.
The pointer starts just past the program and wraps all the way round the core.
When it wraps to 0 it points at ptr itself. Every pass then overwrites ptr with a DAT whose B-field is 0, so the clear stays stuck there and never reaches start.
strengths: Guaranteed to hit every cell of the core.
The self-stopping trick is worth learning.
weaknesses: Slow: one cell per two cycles.
Doesn't stun first, so replicators rebuild behind it.
warriors.tryIt: Add SPL 0 before start so many processes run the clear. Does it get faster? Count how many of the warrior's turns are spent on MOV.

warriors.name: Two-Pass Clear
warriors.inspiredBy: The SPL-then-DAT two-pass clear that finished off Winter Werewolf (W. Mintardjo, 1992) and many later bombers, such as Torch.
warriors.summary: Sweeps the whole core twice: first with SPL 0, which paralyses whatever runs it, then with DAT, which kills it.
how: Pass 1: MOV.I stun, >ptr with DJN counting down exactly one write for each cell that isn't ours.
MOV.AB #len, ptr rewinds the pointer.
Pass 2: MOV.I kill, >ptr, which stops itself on ptr the same way the Sweeper does.
strengths: Beats replicators like Mice: stunned copies can't keep rebuilding.
Simple, and it covers everything.
weaknesses: About 32,000 cycles to finish both passes, so bombers get it first.
Imps survive by crawling over the clear.
warriors.tryIt: Swap the passes: DAT first, then SPL. Which matchups get worse?

warriors.name: Stunner
warriors.inspiredBy: SPL-carpet bombers like Torch (Paul Kline, 1996): bomb with SPL to stun, then clear.
warriors.summary: Drops 999 SPL 0 stun bombs spread widely across the core, then switches to a full DAT sweep.
how: Step 3048 is a multiple of 8, so stun bombs only land a multiple of 8 cells from stun. None of our other instructions is that far away, so we never stun ourselves.
DJN.B loop, #count keeps a counter in its own B-field: the # makes the instruction point at itself.
Once the counter runs out, MOV.I kill, >ptr sweeps the core and stops on its own pointer.
strengths: Stunned enemies barely run while the clear approaches.
Solid all-rounder in the benchmark.
weaknesses: 999 widely spaced bombs still leave most cells untouched.
The sweep at the end is slow.
warriors.tryIt: Try count at 300 and at 1500 and run a 100-round tournament against Silk each time. Is it better to stun more cells, or to start the clear sooner?

warriors.name: Carpet Bomber
warriors.inspiredBy: Unrolled bombing loops of the kind used by fast bombers such as Tornado (Beppe Bezzi, 1996), generated here with a JavaScript loop.
warriors.summary: Drops a "carpet" of 4 bombs in a row, then jumps 16 cells ahead. The JavaScript checks that the carpets can never land on the bomber's own code.
how: A for loop emits N copies of MOV.I bomb, >ptr. Fewer jumps per bomb means more bombs per cycle.
ADD.AB #GAP-N, ptr skips to the next carpet.
The generator throws an error unless GAP divides the core and the carpets fall between copies of the code.
strengths: Bombs on 4 of every 6 cycles, where the Dwarf manages 1 in 3.
Shows constraint checking at compile time.
weaknesses: Covers only 4 cells of every 16.
Larger than the Dwarf, so easier to find.
warriors.tryIt: Change GAP to 12 and recompile. The generator refuses, because 12 doesn't divide 8000. Try 20 instead.

warriors.name: Chameleon
warriors.inspiredBy: P-space switchers, which appeared after P-space joined the ICWS'94 rules in the mid-1990s: warriors that remember between rounds what worked and change strategy after a loss.
warriors.summary: Carries two warriors, Papercut and Gatekeeper. It writes which one it played into P-space, and after a lost round it plays the other. Against any one opponent it settles on whichever wins.
how: LDP.AB #0, res reads the last round's result (0 means it lost), and a second LDP reads the strategy it played.
After a loss it adds 1 to the strategy and takes it modulo 2. A win or a tie keeps it.
STP saves the choice for the next round, and a jump starts either the paper or the scanner.
strengths: Paper beats stones and scanners beat papers, so it has an answer to both.
Learns within a match: it usually loses a round or two at most before settling.
weaknesses: P-space only helps across rounds, so a single round shows nothing special.
Carrying two warriors makes it 47 instructions long.
warriors.tryIt: Battle it against Dwarf for 10 rounds with --report and look for the round where it switches.

warriors.name: Bandit
warriors.inspiredBy: The multi-armed bandit problem from machine learning: how to split your tries between options when you don't yet know which pays best. Built on P-space switchers like Chameleon.
warriors.summary: A three-armed bandit. P-space keeps, for each of three strategies (stone, paper, scanner), the points it has earned and how many rounds it has played. Each round it plays the one with the best average.
how: After each round it adds 0, 1 or 3 points (stored times ten) to the strategy it played, and 1 to that strategy's play count.
It then computes (points + PRIOR) / (plays + 1) for each strategy with DIV. PRIOR is optimistic, so every strategy gets tried before it is judged.
The best average wins. The three arms are a Dwarf-style stone that ends in a core clear, Papercut and Gatekeeper.
strengths: Learns which of rock, paper and scissors beats this opponent, and keeps playing it.
Turns imp matchups that would be losses into ties.
weaknesses: 97 of the 100 allowed instructions: the biggest target in the library.
It needs a few rounds to learn, so short matches favour simpler warriors.
warriors.tryIt: Try PRIOR: 10 (cautious) and PRIOR: 40 (curious) against Imp Ring, and compare the scores over 30 rounds.

warriors.name: Hedgehog
warriors.inspiredBy: The shape of modern stone/imp hill warriors such as Tolypeutes (Roy van Rijn, 2022) and Son of Vain (Oversby and Pihlaja), and of Armadillo (Stefan Strack, 1992) before them: a decoding quickscan, then a booted stone with imps. Written from scratch for ZoreWars; every constant comes from its JavaScript and zorewars tune.
warriors.summary: Three warriors in one. A quickscan checks 24 cells round the core in its first few dozen cycles and carpet-bombs anything it finds. Then it copies a stone far away and starts it there, and launches an 8-process imp spiral. The scan code stays behind as a decoy.
how: Quickscan with decode. Each group of three lines checks four cells: SNE.I compares one pair, SEQ.I <t, … compares a second pair and at the same time decrements a table cell, and a JMP whose B-operand picks one of three table cells. On a find, MUL.B multiplies the chosen table value by a factor D, which lands exactly on the cell that differed.

That only works if every table value v satisfies t + v - 1 = qp + D(v-1) modulo the core size. The JavaScript solves this with a modular inverse, tries every D, and keeps the one that spreads the probes most evenly.
Boot. Sixteen MOV.I lines copy the stone thousands of cells away. Quickscanners that aim at where we loaded find only the old scan code.

Stone. SPL #0 at its top keeps adding processes, so one hit doesn't stop it. All the processes share a bombing loop and a counter. When the counter runs out, one process rewrites the bomb line into a jump, and every process moves on to a core clear. When the clear is done they all idle.
Imp spiral. A jump table sends 8 processes to 8 points a third of the core apart. They move in step, so the spiral repairs single hits, and it turns rounds the stone can't win into ties.
strengths: Our best warrior against the strongest classics when it was added: it beats Agony II and Myrmidon.
Hard to kill: the stone has many processes, the spiral is spread over the whole core, and the decoy wastes enemy quickscans.
weaknesses: 85 instructions: a big target if a scanner finds the right part.
Modern stone/imp and paper/stone warriors such as Tolypeutes and Azathoth still beat it.
warriors.tryIt: Run node cli/zorewars.js compile warriors/hedgehog.js and find the 24 probe cells in the comment at the end. Then set T: 3 for a thinner spiral and see what changes against Gatekeeper.

warriors.name: Hydra
warriors.inspiredBy: The paper/stone shape of Azathoth (John Metcalf) and its AI-tuned successor Arvon: quickscan, boot, then a paper and a stone. Written from scratch for ZoreWars with the same quickscan and stone as Hedgehog.
warriors.summary: Hedgehog's quickscan and stone, with a paper instead of the imps. After the scan it copies the stone and Fast Silk's small paper to two distant spots and starts them: the paper survives almost anything, and the stone does the killing.
how: The quickscan, decode and stone are the same as in Hedgehog.
The boot copies the stone (16 lines) and the paper (8 lines) away with unrolled MOV.Is, then starts one stone process and 2^LEVELS paper processes.
The paper is Fast Silk's loop: every process copies three cells per pass to a new spot and starts the copy.
strengths: Very hard to kill once the paper has spread.
The quickscan still wins some rounds in the first few hundred cycles.
weaknesses: Scanners with SPL carpets, such as Agony II and Gatekeeper, freeze the paper.
89 instructions: the quickscan and boot code make it a big target until it has booted.
warriors.tryIt: Compare Hydra and Hedgehog with node cli/zorewars.js hill warriors/hydra.js --classics: same quickscan and stone, different partner.

warriors.name: Gremlin (ring)
warriors.summary: The volume's Gremlin, moved to the classic ring. It spends nearly all its time on one instruction, DJN.F #10, {-10, which loops on itself while its pointer walks backward through the core, taking one off both fields of every cell it passes.
how: The first four lines start processes and send them on; the stream is line 13, and its pointer is the A-field of line 3 (JMP.B $5).
DJN with an immediate target jumps to itself, so it loops. Each pass, {-10 steps that pointer one cell back, and DJN.F takes one off both fields of the cell it points at.
Clears and stones depend on exact numbers: their pointer, their counter, their bombs. Nudged by one, they write over their own code.
This is the 3D original with only its leftovers changed: each TRN is a NOP and each vector is cut to its x part. The other lines are evolutionary leftovers that run a few times at the start.
strengths: Beats Two-Pass Clear 30-0, Vampire 28-1 and Dwarf 22-7 on the ring.
Alone, it spends 79,971 of 80,000 cycles on the one stream instruction, so there is almost nothing else to break.
weaknesses: Scanners (Gatekeeper, Red Queen, Hedgehog) and papers beat it: 1.18 points per round against the library and the classics.
Papers are many redundant copies, and an off-by-one in a few of them changes nothing.
warriors.tryIt: Run node cli/zorewars.js battle warriors/gremlin.red warriors/twopass.red -r 10 --report and read the clear's ending code: which of its numbers did the stream change?

warriors.name: Plaid
warriors.summary: A stone for the plane. No single step covers a 100×80 torus (a fixed step repeats after at most 400 cells), so Plaid bombs a lattice with two loops: every GX cells along a row, then GY rows down.
how: The inner loop drops a DAT through ptr and adds GX to it, SIZEX/GX times, which brings x back to where it started.
ADD.AB #[0,GY], ptr moves the pointer to the next lattice row.
The first bomb lands half a lattice step below its own row, and every row it bombs is an odd multiple of GY/2 away, so it never hits itself.
The generator refuses a lattice that doesn't divide the plane, or an odd GY.
strengths: Never bombs itself on any plane its lattice fits.
The tuner raised it from 0.87 to 1.00 points per round (GX 4, GY 2).
weaknesses: Its code lies along one row, the row-based attacks' target: Pillar, the same stone standing in a column, beats it 7-3-10.
Stride-based stones fell to about 1.0 points per round on the plane, where linear clears and papers lead.
warriors.tryIt: Run node cli/zorewars.js check warriors/plane/plaid.js --torus 125x64. Why does the generator refuse GX 4 there, and which GX would fit?

warriors.name: Climber
warriors.summary: Code only ever flows along a row, so to travel vertically Climber copies its whole body DY rows down (and DX cells across), then jumps into the copy. The old body stays behind as a decoy.
how: Each copy starts by setting its own src, dst and cnt, because the copy was taken while the original was mid-count.
MOV.I <src, <dst copies the body last cell first; DJN counts the cells.
JMP hop+HOP continues in the copy, where the next hop begins.
strengths: Leaves a decoy body on every row it visits.
Tuning made its hops diagonal (DX 19, DY 45) and raised it from 0.42 to 0.64 points per round.
weaknesses: One process: a single bomb on the live copy ends it.
Papers and clears beat it almost every round (0-10 against Fast Silk, Papercut and Plane Queen, 10 rounds each).
warriors.tryIt: Set DX: 0 so it hops straight down, and compare both with node cli/zorewars.js hill warriors/plane/climber.js --torus 100x80.

warriors.name: Plane Silk
warriors.inspiredBy: Fast Silk's copy loop with two-dimensional copy distances. Its constants come from zorewars tune.
warriors.summary: A small silk paper whose copies jump across rows as well as along them. Each pass copies the body DX cells across and DY rows down, and the distance changes by (EX, EY) every pass, so the copies spread over the whole plane rather than along one stripe.
how: LEVELS SPL 1s start 2^LEVELS processes.
SPL [DX,DY] starts a process in the copy; three MOV.Is copy three cells per pass.
ADD.A #[EX,EY], seed moves the next target, and MOV.F seed, silk resets the pointers before the loop jumps back.
strengths: Nearly unkillable on the plane: in a 17-warrior plane tournament the papers lost 0 to 8 of 320 rounds.
Tuning raised it from 1.99 to 2.15 points per round.
weaknesses: Against other papers almost every round is a tie.
Plane Queen's SPL 0 pass holds it: 1 win, 4 losses and 5 ties in 10 rounds.
warriors.tryIt: Retune it yourself: node cli/zorewars.js tune warriors/plane/planesilk.js --torus 100x80. Does any EY near 0 (copies that stay in a few rows) survive the tuner?

warriors.name: Raster
warriors.summary: A two-pass core clear for the plane. Pointer increments count as plain numbers, so >ptr walks every cell row by row, like a TV raster: first with SPL 0, then with DAT.
how: Pass 1: MOV.I stun, >ptr with DJN counting CORESIZE - 2×SIZEX cells.
Both passes start a row below its own and stop a row above, so Raster never clears its own row.
MOV.AB #[0,1], ptr rewinds the pointer for pass 2 with DAT; then it idles on JMP 0.
strengths: No geometry can hide from it: the counter reaches every cell outside its own two rows.
Linear clears topped the 17-warrior plane tournament: Raster scored 2.15 points per round, second to Two-Pass Clear.
weaknesses: Papers tie or beat it: 0-4-6 against Plane Silk and Fast Silk, 0-6-4 against Papercut (10 rounds each).
Gremlin's stream beats it 0-10.
warriors.tryIt: Run it on the volume: node cli/zorewars.js hill warriors/plane/raster.js --torus 40x20x10. A clear doesn't care about the shape; what changes?

warriors.name: Column Imp
warriors.summary: An imp that crawls down a column instead of along a row. It shows the plane's one new instruction, TRN, which turns a process to face another direction.
how: MOV.I imp, [1,1] puts a copy of the imp in the cell below the TRN.
TRN [0,1] turns the process to face down (+y), so its next instruction is that copy.
The imp, MOV.I 0, [0,1], copies itself one row down and moves there, round its 80-cell column forever.
strengths: Ties most stones and scanners: Dwarf, Stunner and Gatekeeper all 10 ties in 10.
weaknesses: A column is a thin line on the plane: it never kills anything and scored 0.63 points per round against the library (10 rounds each).
Clears and papers beat it: 0-10 against Two-Pass Clear and Fast Silk.
warriors.tryIt: Change TRN [0,1] to TRN [0,-1] and the copy's place to match, so it crawls up. Does direction matter against Raster?

warriors.name: Pillar
warriors.inspiredBy: Plaid's lattice stone, stood on end.
warriors.summary: A lattice stone whose code stands in a column. In every row it is only one cell wide, so row-based attacks such as Plaid's lattice almost never touch it.
how: The body is written as ordinary lines whose operands are vertical offsets: line i refers to line j as [0, j-i].
The launcher copies line i to the cell i+1 rows below the TRN, then TRN [0,1] turns the process to face down.
It runs the body top to bottom; the JMP keeps its heading, so the loop stays vertical. The body bombs a lattice like Plaid's.
strengths: Beats Plaid 7-3-10 head to head, and goes 8-12 against the clears where Plaid goes 2-18.
Tuning to a 2×2 lattice raised it from 0.80 to 1.10 points per round.
weaknesses: Papers beat it every round (0-10 against Fast Silk, Papercut and Plane Silk, 10 rounds each).
Still a stone with one process: one hit on its column ends it.
warriors.tryIt: Run node cli/zorewars.js battle warriors/plane/pillar.js warriors/plane/plaid.js --torus 100x80 -r 20, then watch one round in the arena and see where Plaid's bombs land.

warriors.name: Weave
warriors.inspiredBy: Imp along a row plus Column Imp.
warriors.summary: Imps along a row and down a column at the same time: a moving cross that sweeps one row and one column of the plane over and over. Enemy processes that run into an imp cell become imps too, so rounds it can't win tend to end in ties.
how: SPL down gives the column imp its own process; the first process jumps to the row imp, MOV.I 0, 1.
The second process puts a column imp below a TRN [0,1] and turns onto it, as Column Imp does.
strengths: Turns many stone and scanner matchups into ties.
weaknesses: Almost never wins: 0.73 points per round against the library (10 rounds each), nearly all of it from ties.
Clears beat it: 0-10 against Two-Pass Clear and Plane Queen.
warriors.tryIt: Add a third SPL and a second row imp half a row away. Does a wider net turn any losses into ties?

warriors.name: Plane Queen
warriors.inspiredBy: Found by zorewars evolve --torus 100x80, started from Two-Pass Clear, Papercut and Plane Silk as champions. Lines 3-10 are Two-Pass Clear unchanged; lines 11-17 are Fast Silk's copy loop.
warriors.summary: A two-pass core clear run by two processes, plus a copy loop that leaves one decoy and ends. It was the best warrior on the plane when added: 2.39 points per round against the plane field.
how: Two SPLs start one process for the decoy loop and two for the clear.
The clear is Two-Pass Clear: SPL 0 into every cell, then DAT into every cell, its pointer counting row by row.
Evolution lost the SPL that would start each copy, and the loop's last jump lands on the clear's DAT: it copies three cells once and ends.
That matters: a sprayer that kept looping would be caught by its own SPL 0 pass and fill its own queue, starving the clear.
strengths: Two clear processes survive losing one: worth about 0.15 points per round over Two-Pass Clear.
Scores 2.32 points per round against the 16 classics that can play on the plane.
weaknesses: The decoy adds nothing measurable: without it the warrior scores the same.
Gremlin's stream breaks its clear: 0-30 on the volume.
warriors.tryIt: Delete the first SPL.B $11, $0 and compare with node cli/zorewars.js hill warriors/plane/planequeen.red --torus 100x80. Then delete the second SPL too.

warriors.name: Lift
warriors.summary: An imp that travels through the depth of the volume. After one TRN, every step goes one layer further in, round and round the z axis.
how: MOV.I imp, [1,0,1] puts a copy of the imp one layer in from the TRN.
TRN [0,0,1] turns the process to face +z, so its next instruction is that copy.
The imp, MOV.I 0, [0,0,1], copies itself one layer in and moves there.
strengths: Hard to catch: it tied Two-Pass Clear and Plane Queen in all 10 rounds, and Volume Queen in 8.
weaknesses: Never kills: 0.61 points per round against the library (10 rounds each).
Papers and Leapfrog beat it: 0-10 against Volume Silk, Broadside and Leapfrog.
warriors.tryIt: The evolver invented this same depth imp by itself (warriors/prototypes/evolved-depth-imp.red). Compare the two with node cli/zorewars.js battle and --torus 40x20x10.

warriors.name: Star
warriors.summary: Three imps leaving one point along x, y and z: one crawls along its row, one down its column and one through the layers. Together they sweep three lines of the volume, turning any enemy process they meet into an imp.
how: Two SPLs give it three processes; one jumps straight to the row imp.
The other two each put an imp next to a TRN and turn onto it: TRN [0,1,0] faces down, TRN [0,0,1] faces into the volume.
strengths: Ties most stones and scanners: 0.72 points per round against the library (10 rounds each), nearly all of it from ties.
weaknesses: Never wins a round on its own.
Clears and papers beat it: it lost 8 of 10 rounds to Volume Queen, Papercut and Fast Silk.
warriors.tryIt: Remove the depth imp and run node cli/zorewars.js hill warriors/volume/star.js --torus 40x20x10 before and after. How much is the third axis worth?

warriors.name: Volume Silk
warriors.inspiredBy: Fast Silk and Plane Silk, with copy distances in all three dimensions.
warriors.summary: The small silk paper again, its copies jumping across rows, columns and layers, so they fill the volume rather than one plane.
how: LEVELS SPL 1s start 2^LEVELS processes.
SPL [DX,DY,DZ] starts a process in the copy; three MOV.Is copy three cells per pass.
ADD.A #[EX,EY,EZ], seed moves the next target elsewhere in the volume, and MOV.F resets the pointers.
SIDE can give the JMP's spare operand a free decrement of a far cell; here it changes nothing measurable (±0.01), so it is off.
strengths: One of the volume's strongest warriors: 2.13 points per round on 40×20×10.
Lost no round to a stone, scanner or imp in a 10-round hill run.
weaknesses: Ties other papers nearly every round.
Volume Queen's SPL 0 pass beats it more often than not (1-6-3 in 10 rounds).
warriors.tryIt: Set SIDE: 2 and compare with node cli/zorewars.js hill warriors/volume/volumesilk.js --torus 40x20x10 --seed 4242. Scatter gained from it; does Volume Silk?

warriors.name: Cubist
warriors.inspiredBy: Plaid, with a third loop.
warriors.summary: A stone for the volume. Plaid's lattice stays in its own layer, because its loops never move along z; Cubist adds a third loop and bombs a lattice through the whole volume.
how: The inner loop bombs every GX cells along a row; the middle loop adds [0,GY,0] for the next lattice row; the outer loop adds [0,0,GZ] for the next layer.
Each loop ends where it began on its axis, because each spacing divides its axis.
The first bomb is half a lattice step below its own row and half a step into the volume from its own layer, so it never hits itself.
strengths: Beats the plane's stones and Climber on the volume (Climber 6-0-4, Plaid 4-1-5 in 10 rounds).
weaknesses: 0.64 points per round against the library: a 4×4×2 lattice is too sparse to find papers, and clears reach it first.
Gremlin's stream makes it bomb itself: 0-10, every round a suicide.
warriors.tryIt: Run node cli/zorewars.js check warriors/volume/cubist.js --torus 41x20x9. Why does it refuse, and why can no lattice like this fit a volume with odd sides?

warriors.name: Slant
warriors.summary: A replicator that cuts diagonally through the volume. A bug makes it work better than intended: after its first diagonal hop, each process lays a chain of copies one body length apart and scribbles stray values along a diagonal.
how: Each copy resets its pointers, copies the whole body HOP away (across rows, columns and layers at once) last cell first, and SPLs a process into the copy.
The ADD.AB meant to steer HOP adds to the B-field of the aim line, which is the destination, not the hop.
So from the second pass on the aim line writes the hop value into a cell further along a diagonal each time, and dst keeps pointing at the last copy: each new copy lands right behind the one before.
strengths: Its accidental chains score better than the steering it was meant to have: 1.84 points per round as written, 1.76 with ADD.A.
Beats stones and imps; ties nearly every other paper.
weaknesses: Clears beat it: 1-8-1 against Volume Queen and 0-10 against Plane Queen (10 rounds each).
The free side-effect decrements that help Scatter hurt Slant (1.84 to 1.20), because they land on its own chains.
warriors.tryIt: Change add.ab(imm(STEER), "aim") to add.a, which turns Slant into Scatter, and watch where the copies go in the 3D view.

warriors.name: Scatter
warriors.inspiredBy: Slant with the steering it was meant to have. The free side effect in spare operands comes from Mercenary on ModelWar.ai (studied, not copied).
warriors.summary: Slant as it was meant to work: each process copies the whole body HOP away, starts a process in the copy, then turns HOP by STEER, so every copy lands somewhere new. Alone, it runs code in about 4,400 cells against Slant's 2,000.
how: The copy loop is Slant's: reset the pointers, copy the body last cell first, SPL into the copy.
ADD.A #STEER, aim changes the hop itself (the A-field), so the next copy goes somewhere else.
The SPL and JMP carry a spare operand that decrements a far cell's B-field; every copy runs it from a new place, so the decrements land all over the volume.
strengths: The side effect is worth about 0.06 points per round (1.85 against 1.79 without, 5 seeds).
Beats Leapfrog 10-0 and Battleship 9-0-1 (10 rounds each).
weaknesses: Tuned, it still scores less than Slant (1.76 against 1.84): Slant's chains win.
Clears beat it: 0-10 against Volume Queen and Plane Queen.
warriors.tryIt: Set SIDE: 0 and run node cli/zorewars.js hill warriors/volume/scatter.js --torus 40x20x10 with three seeds. Is the 0.06 bigger than the noise?

warriors.name: Battleship
warriors.summary: A scanner that digs through the volume, checking every cell in turn, and fires a 3D block salvo around anything it finds.
how: The scan is one instruction: JMZ.F dig, >ptr jumps to itself while the cell is empty, and the pointer counts as a plain number, so it walks every cell, row by row and layer by layer.
On a find it aims at the near corner of a block W cells along x, 3 rows down and 3 layers deep, and bombs it with three nested DJN loops.
The dig starts two rows from its own code and SLT stops it two rows short of coming home, so a salvo can't land on Battleship itself.
strengths: Beats stones and clears: 20-0 against Dwarf, 15-5 against Two-Pass Clear.
weaknesses: Papers have too many copies to sink: 0-10 against Mice and Slant, 0-9-1 against Volume Silk (10 rounds each).
One process, one cell per scan step: 1.71 points per round on the volume.
warriors.tryIt: Try BOMB: "spl" (Fleet's choice) and see whether stunning the find helps against papers.

warriors.name: Broadside
warriors.inspiredBy: Fast Silk's three-cells-per-process copy loop, with a bomb line in every copy.
warriors.summary: A small silk paper whose copies bomb as they go. Each pass copies the body somewhere new and drops one DAT one diagonal step further from where that copy is, so many copies bomb side by side along parallel diagonals.
how: The copy loop is Volume Silk's: SPL into the copy, three MOV.Is, then ADD.A and MOV.F to move and reset the target.
MOV.I seed, @hit drops the seed (a DAT) where hit points, and ADD.AB #[BX,BY,BZ], hit moves it one diagonal step on.
The first bomb is off its own row and layer.
strengths: 2.12 points per round on 40×20×10, level with Plane Queen.
Beats stones, scanners and imps, and Leapfrog 7-0-3.
weaknesses: Papers saturate the volume: against other papers almost every round is a tie.
Volume Queen beats it more often than not (1-7-2 in 10 rounds).
warriors.tryIt: Delete the two bomb lines and compare scores. How much does the bombing add to a paper that already survives?

warriors.name: Volume Queen
warriors.inspiredBy: Plane Queen, the evolver's best plane warrior, rewritten as a generator. The qscan mode comes from Pyre-Swept on ModelWar.ai (studied, not copied).
warriors.summary: A two-pass core clear run by two processes, plus a process that sprays N decoys and stops. Its pointer counts as a plain number, so it reaches every cell of the volume. It was the best on the volume when added (2.34 points per round).
how: SPL spray and SPL 1 start one sprayer and two clear processes.
The clear is Two-Pass Clear: SPL 0 into every cell, then DAT, sparing its own code.
The sprayer runs Fast Silk's copy loop N times, leaving fragments of the warrior in other rows and layers, then runs into a DAT and ends, so its own SPL 0 pass can't trap it.
MODE stone sprays DATs instead; MODE qscan probes two pairs of cells first and starts the SPL pass at a find.
strengths: Two clear processes beat one (2.19) and four (0.90).
An evolver run on the volume, started from Plane Queen, ended at the same design: clears are the volume's local optimum.
weaknesses: Its front is predictable and its code never moves: Leapfrog beats it 29-1, and Backdraft and Tripwire 30-0.
Gremlin's stream breaks its numbers and it overwrites its own code (1-29).
warriors.tryIt: Try MODE: "qscan" with node cli/zorewars.js hill warriors/volume/volumequeen.js --torus 40x20x10. Why do four probes rarely find anything?

warriors.name: Leapfrog
warriors.summary: An answer to core clears. A clear can't be hidden from, but its front is predictable and its code never moves. Leapfrog watches a marker on the side the front comes from, and when the front reaches it, copies itself behind the front.
how: It plants a marker SENT rows up, the side a forward clear arrives from.
Its loop clears one cell of its own (forward, from just past itself), then SEQ.I checks the marker.
When either pass of an enemy clear changes the marker, it copies its whole body HOPY rows further up, behind the front, and jumps into the copy. One process, so nothing is left behind to be stunned.
Its own slow clear in time reaches the enemy clear's code, which stays where it started. When its own clear comes round to the marker, it leaps on and starts again.
strengths: Beats every forward clear and stone: Volume Queen 29-1, Plane Queen 28-2, Two-Pass Clear 26-4.
weaknesses: Loses to papers (0-28 against Fast Silk): their copies keep tripping the marker, and they outnumber it.
Blind to a front from the other side: Backdraft and Gremlin beat it 10-0 (10 rounds each). 1.92 points per round overall.
warriors.tryIt: Battle it against Volume Queen with node cli/zorewars.js battle warriors/volume/leapfrog.js warriors/volume/volumequeen.js --torus 40x20x10 -r 5 --report and find the leap in the timeline.

warriors.name: Volume Chameleon
warriors.inspiredBy: Chameleon's P-space switch, playing Leapfrog and Volume Queen's clear.
warriors.summary: A P-space switcher built on the volume's triangle: Leapfrog beats clears, papers beat Leapfrog, and a clear ties papers. It plays Leapfrog, switches to the clear after a lost round, and back after losing with that.
how: LDP reads the last round's result (0 means lost) and the strategy it played, kept at P-space cell KEY.
After a loss it adds 1 and takes it modulo 2; a win or a tie keeps the strategy. STP saves it for the next round.
Strategy 0 starts Leapfrog; strategy 1 starts Volume Queen's clear with two processes. The clear comes first in the code, so it spares everything after it.
strengths: 2.39 points per round on 80×10×10 when added, ahead of Volume Queen and Plane Queen (2.25).
weaknesses: The fastest papers beat Leapfrog outright and can win against the clear too.
Predictable: Anti-Chameleon, which switches after every decided round, beats it 26-2-2.
warriors.tryIt: Run node cli/zorewars.js battle warriors/volume/volumechameleon.js warriors/papercut.js --torus 80x10x10 -r 10 --report and find the round where it switches.

warriors.name: Anti-Chameleon
warriors.inspiredBy: Built to read Volume Chameleon. It carries Volume Silk and Leapfrog.
warriors.summary: A counter-switcher. Volume Chameleon keeps its strategy after a win and switches after a loss, always between the same two. Anti-Chameleon plays a paper or Leapfrog and switches after every decided round, so it is always a step ahead of it.
how: LDP reads the last result (0 lost, 1 won, 2 tied, -1 first round) and the strategy it played.
With SWITCHWIN on, SLT keeps the strategy only after a tie or on the first round; any win or loss switches.
Strategy 0 is Volume Silk's paper (placed last, so its copies take the cells after it); strategy 1 is Leapfrog.
strengths: Beats Volume Chameleon 26-2-2 over 30 rounds.
weaknesses: Against warriors that never switch, switching after a win throws away a winning strategy: 11-12-7 against Volume Queen.
1.98 points per round against the whole field, to Volume Chameleon's 2.33; its paper only ties other papers.
warriors.tryIt: Set SWITCHWIN: 0 (the classic switch-after-loss rule) and compare its record against Volume Chameleon and Volume Queen.

warriors.name: Adapter
warriors.inspiredBy: Leapfrog and Volume Queen's clear in one program.
warriors.summary: Leapfrog whose marker is a sensor. When the marker changes, Adapter looks at what changed it: a clear's front or a bomb means leap; copied code means a paper, so it turns into Volume Queen's clear on the spot. It remembers what it saw in P-space and opens the next round with the answer.
how: LDP reads what it saw last: 0 (a clear, a bomber, or nothing yet) starts Leapfrog; 1 (a paper) starts the clear.
Leapfrog's loop clears one cell, then checks the marker. When it has changed, one JMZ.F on the marker tells the two cases apart: both fields zero is a clear's SPL 0 or DAT 0, or a bomb.
Zero: STP 0, copy the whole program (clear included) HOPY rows up and continue there. Non-zero: STP 1 and start the two-process clear.
strengths: 2.21 points per round on 80×10×10: Papercut 19-6, Battleship 20-10, Volume Queen 20-10, close to even with Volume Chameleon (10-13-7).
Checking both fields matters: matching the clear's exact bombs misread Battleship's DAT $0,$0 as a paper and lost 7-23.
weaknesses: The fastest papers still beat it: 3-5-2 against Fast Silk (10 rounds).
Like Leapfrog, it watches only the side a forward clear comes from: Backdraft and Tripwire beat it 0-10 (10 rounds each).
warriors.tryIt: Make it open with Leapfrog after every loss, to look again. It scored 2.02 instead of 2.21 that way. Find the matchup that costs it most.

warriors.name: Gremlin
warriors.summary: Evolved from random programs by zorewars evolve --scratch: 20 generations on the 100×80 plane, then 12 on 40×20×10, with no library code or opponents. It rediscovered a classic DJN stream that walks backward through memory taking one off both fields of every cell.
how: Almost all its time (79,971 of 80,000 cycles alone) is one instruction, DJN.F #10, {-10, which jumps to itself.
Each pass, {-10 steps the A-field of line 3 one back and uses it as a pointer; DJN.F takes one off both fields of that cell.
A clear depends on exact numbers. Nudged by one, Volume Queen's clear writes over its own code and dies within a few hundred cycles.
The TRNs and vectors are leftovers in lines that never matter, so the same program works on the ring.
strengths: Beats Volume Queen 29-1, Volume Chameleon 26-3, Adapter 28-1, and Plane Queen and Leapfrog 30-0.
A second from-scratch run found a DJN stream again, independently.
weaknesses: Papers shrug it off: they are many redundant copies. 1.87 points per round on 40×20×10.
Its evolver scored it 0.14 against its own ancestors: only the held-out library showed what it could do.
warriors.tryIt: Run node cli/zorewars.js battle warriors/volume/gremlin.red warriors/volume/volumequeen.js --torus 40x20x10 -r 5 --report and read how Volume Queen dies.

warriors.name: Backdraft
warriors.inspiredBy: ULTIMA RATIO REGUM, a 12-instruction backward clear from the public hill archive (n1LS/redcode-warriors, studied, not copied), which scored 2.53 on 40×20×10.
warriors.summary: A core clear that runs backward. Its front arrives from the side forward clears never come from, which every lookout in the library (Leapfrog, Adapter, Volume Chameleon) leaves unwatched. One process lays stun traps, then DATs, each pass stopping just short of itself, over and over.
how: Pass 1: MOV.I stun, <ptr and MOV.I jump, <ptr lay SPL 0 / JMP -1 pairs walking backward. A process on the JMP jumps back onto the SPL.
Pass 2: MOV.I kill, <ptr lays DATs over the same cells.
Each pass is counted to stop just short of its own code; then JMP lap starts again, so it keeps clearing all round.
strengths: The best warrior on both volumes: 2.51 points per round on 40×20×10, 2.36 on 80×10×10.
Beats Leapfrog and Volume Queen 30-0, and papers 13-8 and 14-9.
weaknesses: Gremlin beats it 16-12: a stream breaks a clear's numbers.
The details matter: 2.06 with SPL 0 alone instead of the trap pair, 1.35 with two processes.
warriors.tryIt: Set PROCS: 2 and watch the two processes drift apart. Why does a shared counter split them?

warriors.name: Tripwire
warriors.inspiredBy: After Death, a 1980s warrior from the public hill archive (studied, not copied): a stream that trips its own wire. Gremlin's stream and Backdraft's clear.
warriors.summary: A DJN stream for one lap through the volume, then Backdraft's backward clear. The stream breaks the exact numbers clears and scanners rely on; the clear finishes what a stream can't break, such as papers.
how: DJN.F go, {sp takes one off both fields of a cell and loops, its pointer walking backward.
The wire is a DAT #1, #1 at the very end of its code, the last cell the stream reaches. Taking one off it leaves (0,0), so the DJN falls through.
JMN sees the wire cut and starts the backward clear: SPL 0 / JMP -1 pairs, then DATs, over and over.
strengths: 2.37 points per round on 40×20×10, second to Backdraft.
Beats Backdraft 12-9-9, ULTIMA RATIO REGUM 21-9 and Volume Queen 30-0.
weaknesses: About even with papers.
Gremlin beats it: its own clear has the exact numbers a stream breaks.
warriors.tryIt: Run it alone with node cli/zorewars.js trace warriors/volume/tripwire.js --torus 40x20x10 --last 20: which pass is it in when the round ends? Then make the wire DAT #2, #2 and predict what changes.

warriors.name: Volume Chameleon II
warriors.inspiredBy: Volume Chameleon's switch, carrying Backdraft and Volume Silk.
warriors.summary: A P-space switcher on the new triangle: Backdraft beats nearly everything, a DJN stream breaks Backdraft, and a stream can't hurt a paper. It plays Backdraft, switches to Volume Silk after a lost round, and back after losing with that.
how: LDP reads the last result and the strategy it played; after a loss it switches, and STP remembers.
Strategy 0 jumps into Backdraft (first in the code, so its passes spare everything after it); strategy 1 starts the paper (last, so its copies take the cells after it).
strengths: 2.33 points per round on 80×10×10, second only to Backdraft.
Beats Gremlin 20-6 and Volume Chameleon 27-2.
weaknesses: It has to lose a round to switch, so its first rounds against a stream are played with Backdraft.
Against fast papers it only ties (0-2-8 against Fast Silk, 10 rounds).
warriors.tryIt: Run node cli/zorewars.js battle warriors/volume/volumechameleon2.js warriors/volume/gremlin.red --torus 80x10x10 -r 10 --report and find the round it switches to the paper.

warriors.name: Backdraft II
warriors.inspiredBy: Backdraft, with a wire like Leapfrog's marker on the side a backward stream comes from.
warriors.summary: Backdraft with a wire against DJN streams. When a stream, or anything else, touches the wire, the clear copies itself into cells the stream has already passed and starts again there.
how: A wire cell sits WIRE rows on from its code, the side a backward stream arrives from. Both passes stop just short of it, so only others trip it.
Every step of both passes checks the wire with SEQ.I.
When it has changed, it copies the whole program HOPY rows on and jumps into the copy's first line.
strengths: Turns Gremlin from 10-19 into 12-1-17.
Beats Backdraft and Tripwire 26-4.
weaknesses: Checking the wire every step slows it: 1.91 points per round on 80×10×10, against Backdraft's 2.36.
Forward clears now beat it: 1-19 against Volume Queen (20 rounds, seed 7).
warriors.tryIt: Run node cli/zorewars.js battle warriors/volume/backdraft2.js warriors/volume/volumequeen.js --torus 80x10x10 -r 5 --report and read what kills it.

warriors.name: Fleet
warriors.inspiredBy: Battleship plus Slant: the Red Queen recipe (scanner plus replicator) in 3D. At 31 instructions it needs 80×10×10, where code may be 40 long.
warriors.summary: Battleship's digging scanner and Slant's replicator in one program. The scanner hunts papers' copies while the replicator outlasts the stones that beat scanners.
how: SPL go gives the replicator its own process; the other runs the scanner.
The scanner is Battleship's: JMZ.F on >ptr through every cell, a block salvo of SPL 0s around each find.
The replicator is Slant's, accidental steering included, one process per copy, so it takes few of the scanner's turns.
strengths: Slant's chains suit it: with the steering "fixed" (ADD.A) Fleet drops from 1.66 to 1.16 points per round.
Beats Battleship 10-0 and Gremlin 9-1 (10 rounds each).
weaknesses: Ties papers instead of beating them: in 3D the scanner can't find copies faster than they are made.
Clears beat it: 0-10 against Two-Pass Clear and Volume Chameleon II.
warriors.tryIt: Set BOMB: "dat" and compare with node cli/zorewars.js hill warriors/volume/fleet.js --torus 80x10x10.
